speechtext: Mr. J. P.HOWDEN (St. Boniface) presented the first report of the standing committee on railways and shipping, owned, operated and controlled by the government, and moved that the report be concurred in.

subtopic: MOTION FOB CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I regret that I cannot give consent to this motion, for the reason which I indicated in the committee itself when this question of sitting and having the report concurred in this afternoon was discussed. It would not be convenient for certain members of this committee to attend sittings of the committee when the budget resolutions and supplementary estimates are in the offing for discussion in the house. I desire to make some observations on both, and, if possible, to follow through with the budget resolutions. Therefore, I do not agree to this motion for concurrence. We should be given at least another afternoon in the house, I object to it.

subtopic: MOTION FOB CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext: The purpose of the motion for concurrence is to permit the printing of the proceedings. An understanding was arrived at that there would be no attempt to convene the committee without agreement with the opposition. We cannot proceed with the printing unless this report is adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:

It is a question of law whether a given point is in Canada or outside Canada.
2.	Loss resulting from a concentration of munitions on the American shore is not covered and loss resulting from explosion of munitions being transported on any body of water separating Canada and the United States is not covered unless the explosives are within Canadian territorial waters or being shipped between two Canadian ports as provided by section 14 of the act.

Owing to the fact that not all producers deliver wheat on each successive quota established and owing to the fact that delivery quotas are established on the total authorized acreage at each delivery point, delivery quotas generally provide for the delivery of wheat moderately over space available. Where producers, for one reason or another, do not deliver wheat in accordance with the quotas established, the board follows the practice of making such space available to those producers who do wish to deliver wheat.
On March 18, 1942, about 800 delivery points had delivery quotas closely balanced with available storage. At about 1,300 delivery points, delivery quotas were moderately in excess of storage available and these points included:

(1)	All delivery points where all or part of the 1942 wheat crop is unthreshed. At these points wheat quotas have been advanced to permit the marketing of as much wheat as possible by those producers who threshed last fall.
(2)	All delivery points where available storage, which for one reason or another has not been used and where delivery quotas have been increased for the benefit of those producers desiring to deliver wheat.
(3)	All delivery points where authorized wheat acreage is such that a lower wheat quota would result in waste space. In these cases the quota is increased, even though the next highest delivery quota presses on available space.

QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY MEMBERS FOR ORDER PAPER-MEMBERS' MAIL
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, and arising out of answers to questions on the order paper, I desire to say that some days ago I framed certain questions with respect to an incident which occurred in the city of Halifax a few weeks ago and resulted, I am advised, in the loss of lives of certain members of the Royal Canadian Air Force. These questions have not appeared on the Votes and Proceedings and they are not on the order paper. I have not been approached directly or indirectly by anybody with respect to these questions, but I understand by the grapevine route that they are now in the hands of the censor.
I desire to know whether questions submitted by members of parliament from their places in this house are to be a subject of censorship. If questions are improper, I suggest the head of the department get in touch with the member submitting them to discuss the matter. If there is a reason for it I am sure there is no hon. member but will conform to the course which is desirable, but I do not propose to have any board of censors censoring my utterances in this house or what I shall put on the order paper.
While on this subject of censorship, may I say that I have again been subject to censorship of correspondence addressed to me as a member of the House of Commons by a citizen of this country. I object to that. I took the matter up with the assistant deputy postmaster general, with whom I discussed the matter on previous occasions and with whom I had made what I considered was a very satisfactory working arrangement, but to my surprise I found that the censorship has been transferred from the post office department to the war services department, presumably to give it something to do and justify its existence. I thereupon addressed a letter to the minister, and that letter remains unanswered. Perhaps there has not been time to obtain an answer and submit it to me; I am not complaining about that; that is merely incidental.
My purpose in rising is to say that I have been deprived of a privilege by a board which is not responsible to this House of Commons and I do not propose to stand for it if I can get any support in this house. No board of censors has any right to say that I shall not ask certain questions in this house. The liberty of parliament and of members of parliament is at stake. If we have got to have a fight over this thing, let us have it, for

there is a great principle at stake. I appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I am not very fussy as a rule about these things. What I think ought to have happened is this: if answers to these questions involved the giving of information which would be of aid and comfort to the enemy, it was only necessary to mention it to me. I have a mind and heart and conscience just as keen as that of any other hon. member. But the questions had nothing to do with aid and comfort to the enemy. I will tell you what they had to do with: they had to do with negligence in the operation of the air force, a dereliction of duty, malfeasance on the part of somebody whereby certain young members of the Royal Canadian Air Force lost their lives. The whole thing has been hushed up. Was there a court of inquiry? Was there a coroner's inquest with regard to this incident? This information came to me from one of the most responsible citizens of Halifax, and I want an explanation from somebody. I do not want Colonel 0. M. Biggar or anybody else to say he has authority over what I shall ask. I object to that in the strongest possible terms; and I want the matter looked into and investigated.

Hon. L. R. LaFLECIIE (Minister of National War Services):	I should very
much like to be able to answer all the questions .asked by the hon. gentleman, but I cannot, particularly the last one in which he inquired what one expected to find in his letters. I do not know. subtopic: QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY MEMBERS FOR ORDER PAPER-MEMBERS' MAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to raise a question of privilege in connection with the opening of
Censorship

members' mail. I have found on a number of occasions that constituents and others in Canada are apprehensive about sending letters to members of parliament because they fear they may be opened and their contents revealed). On more than one occasion I have been asked to deliver letters to various people because it was felt that they might be opened. I would ask the government to be good enough to say whether members of parliament and their constituents will be allowed complete freedom in regard to mail. I should like to address a question to the Minister of National War Services in this regard. To whom is the information from the censored letter conveyed? Members of parliament must know what becomes of the information contained in a letter that is censored.
Mr. LaFLECHE: May I assure the hon. member for York-Sunbury and the hon. member who has just spoken that this matter will receive very careful attention. May I suggest to hon. gentlemen of this house that it might be well to wait until one knows before attacking publicly gentlemen who are doing the extremely difficult job of censorship. If my letters had been opened and I thought an injustice had been done to me, I would hold much the same views as certain hon. gentlemen have expressed, but I think realizing the difficult task that these censors have to perform I would first make inquiry. Then if I were not satisfied, I might let go, but it would be after and not before. I shall look into the matter.

subtopic: QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY MEMBERS FOR ORDER PAPER-MEMBERS' MAIL
speechtext:
Would the minister be good enough to declare the policy of the government, and tell us what instructions if any are given to the censors? Is it simply a case of their occasionally opening letters by inadvertence? Do we members of parliament have complete secrecy in connection with our mail? What is the principle involved?
Mr. LaFLECHE: I shall look into the matter and acquaint the hon. member fully with the results. I think that is the only fair way to deal with the question.

subtopic: QUESTIONS SUBMITTED BY MEMBERS FOR ORDER PAPER-MEMBERS' MAIL
speechtext:
This matter was before the house last year. I have had the same experience as my hon. friend. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS OF FINANCIAL PROBLEMS IN LONDON -POST-WAR CURRENCY AND EXCHANGE QUESTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 25 the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more) asked a question concerning the status of international discussions on post-war currency and exchange questions. I now wish to give the formal reply I promised I would give him.
I have been asked a similar question on two previous occasions during this session. In the interval, nothing has occurred which would require any change in the replies I gave on those occasions. I stated previously that- Informal discussions on post-war economic and financial questions have taken place from time to time between Canadian officials and experts from the United Kingdom and the United States, and these discussions will doubtless continue.
Post-war currency, and exchange questions are among matters that have been under discussion. The high commissioner in London,

Right Hon. Anthony Eden
Canadian officials in Washington, and experts from Canadian government departments have participated in these discussions.
I must emphasize again that these discussions are purely informal and exploratory. Their purpose is to bring about an exchange of information and a consideration of problems of mutual interest by experts and officials of the governments of the united nations. Nothing in the nature of a formal conference has been held, and no inter-governmental negotiations have been entered into or are likely to be entered into in the near future. Nothing has occurred which could be construed as in any way binding the Canadian or any other government.

speechtext:
Before the transportation
tie-up occurred in Montreal I endeavoured to compose the differences between the parties. It was only yesterday that the Department of Labour knew the dispute existed. It is one of those disputes known to us as jurisdictional disputes, which are very difficult to settle. These are disputes where one organization already holds an agreement, and another organization is trying to get it away from the first one. I think there is less justification for that strike in Montreal than for any other strike that has occurred since the war broke out. I sometimes wonder when people "go on the street," as we put it in the labour movement, under such conditions as they have done in Montreal, whether they ever think of those youngsters in Tunisia and the men on the sea and under the sea, and what would happen if they acted in the same way.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. C. W. G. GIBSON (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: EXPLANATION AS TO PAYMENT OF DUTY ON PAMPHLETS FROM BRITISH MINISTRY OF INFORMATION
speechtext:
On Thursday last the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) made a statement to the effect that he had received a parcel of pamphlets from the British Ministry of Information in New York on which he had been required to pay duty on an appraised value of S15. He went on to state that the impression given was "that it was an effort on the part of the government to stop British propaganda."
view of the fact that this statement was picked up by various newspapers, and was the subject of an editorial in the Ottawa Journal on Saturday last, I should like to make a statement in regard to the matter.
The material described by the hon. member as being pamphlets from the British Ministry of Information, of no commercial value and not for resale, is not subject to duty. As recently as February 18 the customs officers at our main ports were reminded that such material was entitled to free entry. On investigating the circumstances surrounding this entry I found that the parcel had arrived at the Ottawa customs office by express and was cleared on March 15. Many of our experienced customs officers are serving at the present time in the forces. The ofiicer on duty in the express parcels branch happened to be away on sick leave on that day. An officer from the customs freight branch was acting in his place and was not aware of the previous rulings that had been made in cases of this kind. As a result, he applied the duty applicable to printed matter 
and pamphlets generally. I regret very much that a mistake such as this should have occurred, and the hon. member will of course receive a refund of the duty and taxes that were paid.

subtopic: EXPLANATION AS TO PAYMENT OF DUTY ON PAMPHLETS FROM BRITISH MINISTRY OF INFORMATION
speechtext: That is not . the point.

subtopic: EXPLANATION AS TO PAYMENT OF DUTY ON PAMPHLETS FROM BRITISH MINISTRY OF INFORMATION

subtopic: EXPLANATION AS TO PAYMENT OF DUTY ON PAMPHLETS FROM BRITISH MINISTRY OF INFORMATION

The British form is "Ministry of Information". I questioned this at the time. I made no attempt to bring the matter up until I had taken it to the senior officer at the customs branch and got his stamp on the form. The customs officers discussed it together and it seemed to me that this was a definite ruling of the department, so I brought it up in the house.

maintopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH WHEAT BOARD-PRICES- PREMIUM ON FEED WHEAT-PERMITS FOR EXPORT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH WHEAT BOARD-PRICES- PREMIUM ON FEED WHEAT-PERMITS FOR EXPORT
speechtext: In view of the reports which appeared in the western newspapers on March 13, and on two occasions since that time, that the wheat board was in Ottawa conferring with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) in regard to ways and means of making it possible for the western producers to receive at least a portion of the recent increase in the price of wheat, is the minister now prepared to inform the house what policy or plans have been agreed upon? I may add that I conferred briefly with the minister, and I think he is in a position to make a statement to-day. Perhaps at the same time he will deal with the matter of the eight cent premium or subsidy on wheat sold by the producers for feed purposes, and he might also say a word with regard to the permits that have been issued for the export of our wheat to the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH WHEAT BOARD-PRICES- PREMIUM ON FEED WHEAT-PERMITS FOR EXPORT
speechtext:
I am afraid I shall have to disappoint the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) if he expects me to-day to answer all the questions he has raised. However, I did intend to make a very brief statement, a progress report, on discussions which the government have been holding with the members of the wheat board and others during the past week or two.
During this time the government has been giving consideration to a number of matters in connection with the marketing of grain and I should like to inform the house of two decisions which have been made to date. The government has instructed the Canadian wheat board to permit the marketing of all durum wheat produced in 1942 in the west. As the house knows, marketings of wheat in the west in 1942-43 are restricted to 280,000,000 bushels, which will work out at fourteen bushels per authorized acre. Owing to the shortage of durum wheat the board has permitted the marketing of fourteen bushels per authorized acre since early in the crop year. Under the fourteen bushel limitation a little over two million bushels of durum wheat have been marketed in the west, but this has not been sufficient to meet national requirements. By removing the restriction on the marketing of durum wheat for the balance of the present crop year it is expected that an additional two million bushels will be delivered in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.
Perhaps I should give some further explanation of the reason for this decision. Durum wheat is used principally for the manufacture of macaroni, which is in demand for both civilian and military use. At this time macaroni is especially important not only because of its value as a food product but because in its use it becomes a substitute for meat. The government therefore decided to keep up the production of this food product made from durum wheat. I might add that durum wheat is not a bread wheat and therefore is in fact a different product from the bulk of the wheat produced in the west. The relaxing of the restrictions on the marketing of durum wheat is for the balance of the present crop year only, and the restrictions on wheat marketings announced for 1943-44 will apply to durum wheat as to other varieties on and after August 1, 1943.
I now come to a matter which affects a small proportion of the wheat producers of the west. During the past few months a considerable number of producers who were operating farms in 1942, and who held 194243 permits to market grain, have enlisted in

Mobilization Act

the armed forces. In some cases producers of 1042 have been drafted for military service. In a large proportion of these cases where producers who operated farms in 1942 have entered the service of this country, there is a balance of grain which cannot be marketed during the present crop year under restrictions now in effect. In many cases this grain would be left without adequate protection during the owner's absence on military service. The government has decided to authorize the Canadian wheat board to permit delivery of the balance of the 1942 crop belonging to 1942 permit holders who have joined the armed forces within the crop year. This instruction to the Canadian wheat board will apply only to the permit holder's grain and not to any share of the crop which may belong to anyone else interested in the farm. For instance, if the permit holder rents a farm on a half-crop share basis, only the balance of the permit holder's grain will be deliverable on his entering military service. The landlord's share of the crop will continue to be subject to the usual restrictions.
Not a great many producers will be affected by this ruling. Most enlistments in the west in rural areas are young men of farm families who do not operate farms of their own. Where farm operators of 1942 holding 1942-43 permits do enter the service of their country, the government feels that it should cooperate in leaving their affairs in as good shape as possible by giving them the opportunity to market the balance of the grain, which is legally their property, on their farms.
Other decisions in regard to grain are being formulated and will be announced to the house at a very early day.

On that assumption I may have misinformed my colleague. After all it is not an important matter whether the letter was written after Mr. MacNamara's letter went out or before. The fact is that it was written on the same subject matter, and I think the minister will agree that it contained a splendid statement of the position and ought to be included in the file, if technically it was not included.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am glad to hear that. These are questions which the western farmer wants to have answered, and I do not want to return to my constituency for the holidays without having the answers. That is one reason why I am rising to-day. I think the government should give us the answers.
Food is becoming more important in the war effort. Two years ago there was no idea that we would face a food shortage either in Canada or in the United States. The situation has changed and we may be facing within the next year a real food shortage. I do not believe that the policy outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to western grain is one which will tend to increase our food supplies. I have in my hand the last issue of Maclean's magazine, of April 1, which contains a whole editorial dealing with this matter of food. The article is headed "Food may win the peace." I quote from it in part:
To-day, in both Canada and the United States, the warnings are up. A food shortage is not only possible, it is inevitable unless exceedingly rapid action is taken to remove the cause.
Britain, in spite of the tremendous advances in her own agricultural production, in spite of mounting shipments from this side of the ocean, during the winter had to dip into her reserves.
I shall not quote further except to add that the editorial says that the main cause is the man-power shortage. I agree that that is one of the causes, but I should like to go a little more deeply into the present man-power situation in relation to agriculture. The manpower shortage on the farm exists not solely on account of enlistments, but because there has been during the last two or three years an exodus of farm help and small farmers to manufacturing centres to work in industries because they can get much better remuneration there than on the farm. Prices of many manufactured articles have been fixed on a cost-plus basis. The first war contracts for ships, aeroplanes and other equipment necessary to the war were let on a cost-plus basis. Wages were allowed to rise in those industries to eighty and ninety cents an hour, which is a higher rate than agriculture can possibly pay. With present prices of agricultural products all that the farmer in western Canada can afford to pay is from forty to fifty dollars a month.

The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has stated that he expects to return as many as 200,000 men from manufacturing industries to the farms. He will experience a great deal of difficulty if he expects a man who is receiving eighty or ninety cents an hour in industry to go back to the farm to work for forty-five or fifty dollars a month. Until prices of agricultural products are brought into line with those of the products of industry in this country and the farmer enabled to pay his labour the same wages as industry pays, we are likely to' have serious difficulties in maintaining our present rate of production. And feed is necessary. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, said that feed was the determining factor in the amount of agricultural produce which we could raise in Canada, and I believe he was right. It is impossible to produce milk, beef, butter and cheese unless we have feed. His statement was that in August, 1942, we had only one month's supply of feed on hand, and that therefore it would have been impossible, no matter what action the government had taken prior to that, to produce more agricultural products than were produced. If feed is the determining factor in this respect, we in Canada need a policy which will facilitate provision of the largest possible amount of feed. I do not believe that the policy outlined by the minister and brought down in the first days of this session is such a policy, and I intend to compare it with what has been suggested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
Before doing so, however, I shall give a few figures as to the production of grains in this country during the last year or two. I do not think the government can take credit for the large additional production which we had in 1942. Credit must be given to the government for the increase in acreage, but not for the per acre production. Here are comparative figures:

These figures furnish proof positive that it was climatic conditions during 1942 which gave

Western Grain Crop
us the additional production. It is my contention that we shall use a large part of this production during the coming year in the feeding of our live stock. We shall not have a very large carryover of coarse grains at the end of the year. There will be a considerable carryover of wheat and flax, but we would not have it if we were able to export to the United States the coarse grain for which they are asking. Something will have to be done to get greater production if we are to have the necessary supplies.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture made certain definite recommendations to this government for a grain policy for 1943. The federation is not composed entirely of westerners; indeed they are in a minority in it. It includes representatives of the dairymen of Quebec and eastern Canada, the apple growers of Nova Scotia and British Columbia, poultry producers, live stock breeders, and cooperative organizations. The federation is thoroughly representative of Canadian agriculture, and its recommendations are not those of one section or group but of national agriculture as a whole. It is certain that the federation does not agree with the policy which the government brought down. The best expression I have seen of their opinion is contained in the March issue of the Country Guide. This magazine is the official organ of the grain growers association of western Canada, in which the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) obtained his start in life; and they have not been-to say the least-against the government. Nevertheless they have this to say;
If a satisfactory explanation has been forthcoming of the slap in the face administered to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture by the federal government it has not come to the attention of the Country Guide. The federation was in the second day of its annual meeting at Calgary. When the afternoon papers came out they carried the announcement of the government's wheat policy for the 1943 crop. This national farmers' organization, representing every important branch of the industry across Canada, had every reason to believe that it was recognized by the government as the authentic voice of Canadian agriculture. After its annual meeting two years ago its delegation was received by Mackenzie King and 11 members of his cabinet. Last year, its spokesmen received the same respectful hearing. The federation expected, and had a right to expect, that, with respect to the greatest agricultural problem in Canada, the government's announcement would be withheld until it had had an opportunity to present its views, as on former occasions.
Instead, the federation was completely and rudely ignored. The government waited until it was in session so that there would be no doubt about it. It was a piece of studied, cynical insolence. It was also a display of blundering politics. The government has been in trouble enough with the farmers. It should invite their cooperation and good-will. One way
to get it is to show respect for their national organization, an organization which has a larger affiliated membership, and is more representative of every phase of Canadian agriculture, than any other organization of farmers in Canadian history.
I should like to compare the policy laid down by the minister with that suggested by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The first point in the policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this chamber on January 29 was this:
1. The fixed initial price of wheat under the Canadian Wheat Board Act will remain at 90 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur or Vancouver.
The suggestion of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in this regard was as follows:
We reaffirm our recommendation of last year that the initial price to be paid by the Canadian wheat board for wheat should not be less than one dollar per bushel basis No. 1 northern in store at lakehead or Vancouver. We recommend that for the benefit of the producer all wheat sold for domestic consumption should realize not less than $1.35 per bushel.
There is considerable difference there. A special advisory committee has been appointed to advise the wheat board with regard to the marketing policy in western Canada. We have never had a statement from the government as to what that board's recommendations were. In making his statement I wish the minister would indicate what the recommendations of the advisory committee were. It seems to me the farmers of western Canada have a right to know about those recommendations; otherwise they have no knowledge as to whether or not the committee is really representing them.
The second point made by the minister was with respect to the quota. He stated the quota would be 280,000,000 bushels as of last year, and that the delivery would be on the basis of fourteen bushels per acre. This is the one point on which the federation of agriculture agreed with the minister. They agreed that in western Canada we should have a quota of 280,000,000 bushels, and that it should be allotted as formerly among the farmers in western Canada. There is this point, however, that if there is a failure in certain sections of the west the government will not be accepting 280,000,000 bushels, in connection with its announcement in whereby it makes provision for fourteen bushels per acre, for seeded acreage. But I doubt whether that will be the case, because I believe there will be a carryover of this year's wheat sufficient to fill the quota, despite any failure in crop we may have this year.
The third point outlined by the minister had reference to payment for storage for grain
Western Grain Crop

on farms. He made it clear it was the intention of the government to cease payment of Storage for grain stored on farms. The recommendation of the federation of agriculture was as follows:
We regret that the government did not accede to the request of western farm organizations to continue this year the payment of farm storage on a basis corresponding to that of the previous year, and believe that such payment should be a continuing part of the government's wheat policy.
Speaking in the house before, I said I did not believe the reasons given by the government were sufficient to warrant its stopping payments for storage. The chief reason given was that the farmers were not bringing forward their wheat, and that there was empty space available. It was pointed out that to have the wheat moved in the proper season, so as not to have a congestion around the first of August, when the new crop was coming on, the government would have to cease payment of storage, and more or less force the farmer to deliver his wheat. I know from personal experience that in many parts of western Canada wheat was not being delivered because the space available in the elevators was not for the grade of wheat the farmers had on hand. In many places there are only two or three elevators, in which would be bins for No. 3, No. 4 or No. 2 wheat, when the farmer might have No. 5 or No. 6. In those circumstances he could not make delivery. Much wheat was held back on that account.
I know, too, that a considerable amount of wheat was held back so that the farmers could make delivery to their own elevators. They may have been accustomed to delivering to the pool, and they held back their wheat until space was available in pool elevators for them to make delivery, despite the fact that there might have been other elevators with available space. This payment for storage of grain on farms should be continued. It is one of the government's policies which I believe was good. It tended to encourage farmers to hold their grain off the market during the rush season in the early part of the year, thus obviating a procedure which has always been detrimental to farmers' interests in western Canada,
The fourth point in the minister's policy as outlined in the house was with respect to the fixed price on flaxseed. He said that the fixed price for flaxseed in 1943 would be continued at $2.25, basis in store Fort William, Port Arthur. The recommendation of the federation of agriculture was as follows:
In view of the hazards associated with flax production the guaranteed price for flax should be increased from $2.25 to at least $2.50 a bushel. We feel that the objective, announced

at the conference last December, of a transfer of one million acres of western land from wheat to flax should be maintained. Any flax production in excess of available crushing capacity could be stored in one-half the space which would be required for the product of a corresponding wheat acreage. Any surplus of flaxseed production which might arise would simply mean a desirable transformation of a portion of its surplus into a more desirable form.
Production of flaxseed in Canada this year is approximately 16,000,000 bushels. One return I received showed that we have a crushing capacity for 5,000,000 bushels, and another showed that it was for 6,300,000 bushels. That means we shall have approximately 10,000,000 bushels of flax in Canada this year for which we have no crushing capacity. The only available mills I know of are in the United States, and I suppose that flax will be exported to the United States for crushing. The price of flax in the United States is $2.98 a bushel; and when we add to that the exchange the price is brought up to approximately $3.25, or $1 over the Canadian price.

There is this profit to be made out of the export of flax, from which the western farmer is not receiving any benefit at the present time. I do not know how much has been exported, but I have asked for that information in a question on the order paper. Certainly if the wheat board is handling and exporting our flax it must be making a nice profit, and the producers in western Canada want to know why they should not receive the benefit of that price.
The sixth point in the minister's programme had to do with the payment of the acreage bonus. His suggestion was that $2 per acre should be paid on the basis of the acreage taken out of wheat, using the 1940 acreage as a basis. The recommendation of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in this respect is as follows:
We recommend that a bonus of $4 per acre be paid on land taken out of cultivation and seeded to grass and continued at $2 per acre per year for two additional years provided this land remains in grass.
The federation had a further proposal with regard to advances for grain in storage. They
say:
The federation regrets that the government has not acceded to the request of grain producers that provision be made for a system of

Western Grain Crop
advances against deliverable grain in store on the farm. Lack of such credit facilities have imposed undue hardships in certain sections and in anticipation of similar conditions occurring the coming crop year, we suggest that further consideration be given this recommendation.
In the United States they have had such a system working successfully for a number of years whereby on grain stored in granaries which are locked advances are made to the farmers. Such a provision would be of benefit in'Canada in the financing of a crop.
There is a question arising out of the statement the minister made a few moments ago with regard to the quota. What share of the quota of fourteen bushels per acre belongs to the landlord? If a man has bought land on a one-third crop payment basis, does he have to deliver one-third of fourteen bushels per acre to the landlord or may be deliver the full fourteen bushels himself leaving the landlord's share in the granary? I do not think there is any decision on that point, and it is one of considerable interest and should be clarified.
When we compare these two policies it is easy to see how during the next year we may get a considerable reduction rather than the increase that we desire in the production of food in Canada. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) said that these continual pressures being brought to bear against the price ceiling are injurious to the country. I would point out that if prices of agricultural products had been frozen at a fair level, these pressures would not be brought to bear. I would point out two or three ways in which prices for western agricultural products might be increased without affecting the price ceiling. Take barley, for example. At the present time we have a premium of 5 cents a bushel for malting barley. The premium in the United States and Great Britain is much greater than this. In Great Britain, according to one of the agricultural papers in western Canada, the price paid for malting barley is 35 shillings per long hundredweight, which amounts to something like $3.36 a bushel. I can see no reason why a premium of 15 cents a bushel would affect the price ceiling in this country. In fact, according to a statement made in this house by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) some two years ago, there are thirty-five to thirty-six pounds of malt in each bushel of barley. The government collects 12 cents a pound excise tax on that malt, or about $4.20 excise tax on every bushel of barley malted in Canada. In view of that I do not see why the farmers should not receive a larger premium than they are getting to-day.
Then, in regard to the ceiling on flax, I do not see how a better price for flax would seriously affect the price ceiling in this country, though it would put greater purchasing power in the hands of western farmers. As to the use they would make of that money I do not believe it would tend toward inflation. There is a tremendous debt burden in western Canada, and that additional money would be largely used for retiring debts, leaving the farmer in a better financial position after the war and enabling him to buy a few war bonds.
It appears to me that the farmer has been left to bear too large share of the load. Present prices of beef are out of line with prices in the United States. The price of beef cattle in the United States to-day is $16 per 100 pounds; in Canada it is $1125. Dressed hogs in the United States are $19.50 to $20; in Canada, $16.15.

As a result of the export of beef cattle to the United States, the producers in this country are having to subsidize the consumer, and again the growers of feed and feed grain in western Canada through the lower ' prices they are receiving are having to subsidize to a certain extent beef producers in this country. In view of these facts and in view of the necessity for greater production of feed in this country, the government would be well advised to reconsider its policy as announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the first day of this session. To that end I move an amendment seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas):
That all the words after "that" he struck out and the following substituted:
"This house desires to record its opinion that before the marketing policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on January 29 with respect to the 1943-44 crop is put into effect it be revised to bring it into conformity with the needs of agriculture so that the latter may be enabled to make its full contribution to the war effort."
I have just a few more words to say in regard to inflation. I believe that shortages in this country are more likely to produce inflation than higher prices to the farmers.
If we are to be short of many food products, it will be much harder to control inflation than under conditions whereby you are giving to the people who produce the food of this country their cost of production, thereby enabling them to produce more food than at the present time.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to support what the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has said, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize one particular point. Apparently as far as agriculture is concerned the policy of the government has been that we cannot have guns and butter. It is time the government changed that policy and realized that you must have butter before you can have guns. Bread and butter are just as necessary as anything else in the production of guns, just as important as aluminum and oil in producing the munitions of war.
We in this group have constantly urged the government to attack this food problem on this basis, to take into consideration the man on the land, and in these days the women on the land who are doing a great deal of land work and getting no reward for it. Food is the life-line of war, and the sooner we realize that fact the better. It is too bad it has not been realized much sooner.
There is every evidence to-day that we are facing a critical food shortage. Last year about 450 people representing one of our greatest agricultural provinces came here to plead their case. They asked for justice; they asked to be allowed to continue their work in order to make their contribution to the winning of the war. They realized the necessity of food apparently to a much greater extent than the government realized it, to judge by the actions of the government subsequent to that time. That deputation received very little encouragement, but they went back home and kept on working. They overcame obstacles that seemed insurmountable, and at times it almost seemed that these obstacles were being deliberately placed in their way. They carried on without parity prices, without sufficient labour, without

consideration from the government. They had to face mounting costs in every field. If they went to buy machinery they found that the cost had increased. The cost of repairs also continued to increase, in spite of what was supposed to be a price ceiling throughout the country.
One of the basic mistakes in connection with the freezing of prices in Canada at the beginning of the war arose from the fact that prices of agricultural commodities were completely out of line with agricultural costs of production. Had this difference been levelled off, there would have been very little trouble by way of demands of this kind, and the farmer would have "been able to carry on without having to face this particular problem. The farmer is compelled to accept certain price ceilings, but he has not been guaranteed any bottom to prices. In many instances he has been encouraged to go into the production of such commodities as eggs; then, after prices have risen to & fairly decent level, suddenly those prices drop and he is left holding the bag. The farmer himself usually asks- for direction; when the government said, "We want flax," the farmer got busy and produced it. In 1942 the government told the farmer, "Go out this year and produce coarse grains. We will take all you can grow. We need them in this country for the production of meat and dairy products. They need them in the United States; in fact the world is short of coarse grain." Accordingly last year the farmer went out and, aided by favourable weather and good growing conditions, produced one of the greatest crops ever harvested in this country. Then the government put it under a quota.
That crop has harvested in the face of tremendous difficulties. I personally visited a number of farms last year and saw what was going on. I recall that on one farm I visited there was a threshing crew consisting of one man and five women. Another threshing crew was made up of two men and three girls of about sixteen or seventeen years of age. I assisted in combining a field, and the boy who wras driving the tractor was only twelve years old, but making a splendid job of it. These people have been carrying on in the face of difficulties, and they have been producing to a remarkable extent. Their efforts have not been appreciated. I am of opinion that when the food shortage strikes this country, as apparently it will, Canada will suddenly realize the great job the farmers have been doing and the many difficulties they have had to face in order to carry on.
Our production of wheat in 1942 was in excess of 560,000,000 bushels. According to the

Western Grain Crop
bureau of statistics, up to about February 25 last some 164,500,000 bushels had been delivered, leaving about 400,000,000 bushels in storage on the farms. Last year at this time they were storing only some 130,000,000 bushels; and there is still a portion of the wheat that has not been threshed. According to the hon. member for Melfort the production of oats for 1942 amounted to 616,000,000 bushels, and up to the present time only about
63.090.000	bushels have been delivered. According to the hon. member the barley production was 272,000,000 bushels, of which only some 47,000,000 bushels have been delivered. This all means that to-day the farmer is carrying stored in his bins over 1,000,000,000 bushels of grain. Under the policy of this government he is not to be granted any payment for that storage. He is growing this grain at a loss, and he is being compelled to store it without payment. Consider the position of a man engaged in the production of munitions. What would happen to that man if, after manufacturing his products, the government said, "Well, we have no room for your goods. Our boats are all full, so that we cannot take what you have made. We have not enough shipping to carry it away, so that you will have to store it yourself, and we will not pay you for it." How long could any war industry carry on under those conditions?
I should like to mention a typical case in order to illustrate what I mean. Here is a farmer who for obvious reasons we will call Mr. Sharp. He has a section of land, with 520 acres under cultivation. He knows that Canada needs food, and he knows all about the shortage of beef and dairy products. He has fifty-three head of pure-bred beef cattle, six milch cows and twelve brood sows. He has more than enough feed to finish off this number of cattle and twice the number of hogs he will raise. This year he threshed
5.000	bushels of wheat and 4,000 bushels of coarse grain. On the farm there is this man, fifty-eight years of age; two sons, twenty-four and twenty-six years of age, and his wife and daughter, who also assist in the work of the farm. He and the boys are expert farmers, capable of doing everything required on that farm. He has the labour; he has a tractor, and all the other farm machinery. Here is a complete plant, with experienced, technically skilled labour to carry on the big job of producing the food we need in this country and overseas. He has everything essential for the production of beef, pork, butter, dairy products and bread. This man must have a certain amount of cash in order to carry on his business. Anyone who knows anything about
agriculture or any other business knows that a cash return is essential in order that operations may be carried on.
This man has a note of S800 to meet at the bank, and he must pay taxes of over S300. He has a large threshing bill to pay; he must buy his oil and gasoline and pay for repairs on his tractor and farm machinery. He has a balance due on his tractor, and he must pay also for operating his house and the cost of medical and dental services. He will require approximately
82,000	in cash as income for the year. In a return tabled to-day it is stated that at 1,300 delivery points the quotas are in excess of the storage facilities available. I have come across this fact quite frequently. These men say that while there is a quota of fourteen bushels, there is no room in the elevators for more than five bushels per acre. Many of them I find have not been allowed to deliver more than the first five-bushel quota. How can they meet their expenses when they have no other means of obtaining cash? They are being pressed by their creditors. What are they to do?
There is only one thing for a farmer to do. He must turn around, as this man did, and sell forty head of his stock, milch cows, calves, feeders, the very basis from which the future meat production of this country should come. He has had to sell these cattle at a time when he has feed grain stored on his farm, when he has his boys there to do the work. He had his herd in production, but he was forced to sacrifice the meat production of this country as a result of the marketing policy of this government. He kept only three brood sows and got rid of the other nine.
What is the policy of this government with regard to food? What are they doing about such situations? We are told that they have the matter under consideration, but the farmer is starting his 1943 production. Has he any policy upon which he can work? None whatever. There are several problems mixed up with this matter. One is the question of debt, with which I hope we shall deal shortly. The other is the matter of manpower. In this particular case, one of the boys was anxious to do his bit and tried to enlist in the air force. He was told that they had no room for him but that they would call him just as soon as there was room. He went back to the farm to wait for his call from the air force, and in the meantime both sons received calls to report for compulsory military service.
They made application for postponement, but they were refused. What is the position of that father, the man in charge of that farm? These refusals have placed him in a position

Western Grain Crop

where he has lost all hope of being able to carry on. He told me that he would just about have to quit and fold up. After considerable correspondence we were able to get one postponement granted until further notice, but that still leaves the father in a position where he does not know what will happen. He does not know whether the boy will be called up on July 1, after the crop is in or whether he will be allowed to stay on until the crop is harvested.
The farmer in the west is storing a considerable quantity of this grain which will be used in this country in the near future. Of the
560.000.	000 bushels of wheat we had last year, the government will take only 280,000,000 bushels, and the farmer is storing the other
280.000.	000 bushels. If this grain were held in the elevators at the head of the lakes the government would be paying storage, but apparently 'no storage is to be paid to the man who has grown the grain and is storing it in bins which he has built himself. That is the present policy.
I advocate that storage should be paid on the undelivered fourteen bushels per acre quota. This would be paid, provided that the farmer stored it in bins which could be inspected and sealed. They would have to be inspected to make sure that the rain was kept out and that there was no leakage. The government would then pay the farmer an advance of seventy cents a bushel at the farm. That wheat would be the property of the wheat board, and the farmer would be paid the difference when it was eventually delivered.
This would provide the farmer with the cash he needs. At the present time he cannot deliver his grain because there is no room in the elevators. The government have told us that transportation difficulties prevented them from hauling the 50,000,000 bushels, for which I understand they have space. But that is not the fault of the farmer, and he should not have to curtail his whole production scheme on account of that shortage. I have here a little piece taken from the Western Producer, of November 3, 1942. It puts the case better than I could do in the few moments at my disposal. I am reading it for the benefit of the stooges of the grain trade who may be here.
First they should go over their records for, say, the last thirty years.
This is dealing with the grain companies. From these a list of all their patrons together with the amount of grain each delivered can be drawn up. From the data thus assembled shares in the company proportionate to deliveries may be issued to all the patrons. (There would be some adjustments for those who had died, retired or moved away, but these details would be easily adjusted.) Next the company officials should mark out suitable geographical units and notify the new shareholders in each to call a meeting to select a specified number of delegates to assemble in Winnipeg on a certain date. When that meeting had been called to order the president and general manager of the company should ascend the platform and, first of course having acquired

the consent of the old shareholders, should ceremoniously burn all the old shares in full view of the assembled farmers. Then in due and correct legal order they should transfer sole ownership and control over all the properties and vest them in their former patrons as represented by the delegates assembled in the hall. That done, all former officials should remove themselves from the premises and property of the company for ever unless their services are requested by the new owners. Then, after a few years' experience in the technique of operation, the new company would be a fairly close approximation to the existing wheat pools.
This is a simple procedure and it has behind it that element of equity and fair dealing without which any enterprise has little merit. For it is a fact that the farmers by their patronage have paid for the elevators and for all the other properties of the private companies. They have also paid the salaries and the profits. How then could justice be better served than by handing over to them that which is theirs by right, if purchased two or three times over?
In connection with the wheat pools, let me say that, contrary to a charge made by the hon. member for Wood Mountain on July 30 last, they would never be owned by four or five people at the top. The charge he then made I want to refute now, and to state that the pools have been, are, and will be owned by those who patronize the elevators. My experience has been that if you want to get a square deal when selling your grain, take it to your own pool elevator.
Speaking in this chamber on March 22, the hon. member, as reported in Hansard, at page 1448, said:
I wish to refer to something that has happened to myself and several others in Saskatchewan in regard to this cooperative elevator matter. When the Saskatchewan cooperative elevators started, in order to build elevators, they took two cents a bushel from all the people who gave them wheat to handle, . . .
That is nothing new. We had to have money from some source to build elevators or purchase them; this is the means which was taken, and all w'as going well up to the time of the 1929 man-made depression. I say "manmade" because it was not natural; it was planned some time ahead, and farmers and others were the victims.

Remember that people were asked to produce this year 280,000,000 bushels of wheat, which works out to fourteen bushels per acre quota, and now those who happened to grow durum wheat in a big way, and also hard wheat, and have marketed their fourteen bushels to the acre quota, are entitled to market also all the durum wheat they have on hand. Those people, with their harvesting machinery,

went back to assist their neighbours in harvesting operations. I do not have to tell farmers here about the difficulties they had in paying their harvesting expenses, under the then existing quota set-up.

That was distinctly refused. Picture the hardship some of those people had to undergo in arranging to pay for help, and for the usual operations of their machinery, for gasoline, and so on. They certainly had great difficulty in financing their undertaking. After all that, the other man, who was able to sell fourteen bushels is allowed, as stated this afternoon by the minister, to sell an unlimited quantity of durum wheat he may have grown or purchased over and above that. Certainly this adds to all the confusion our farmers are experiencing at the present time. And when one thinks that within less than thirty days in many places the people will be on the land attempting to produce another crop, we must conclude that that is not what they arc entitled to.
On other occasions I have spoken about the on-again off-again policy of the government concerning flax production. A statement was given to the public by a group of experts, who met in Winnipeg early in March, to the effect that the requirements are much greater than asked for by the Minister of Agriculture in his last statement. The question of farm debt legislation was raised by my colleague the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) on March 2. The government seemed a bit bewildered when the question was raised, and promised that a statement would be made within the next few days. In that same week, namely on March 5, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) rose in his place and said that in view of the fact that he' expected a delegation representative of the three prairie provinces, within the next few days, he did not think he should make his statement for some time.
In due course that delegation, consisting of representatives of the governments of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, came to Ottawa. I believe they met the Prime Minister, and other ministers of the cabinet concerned with this matter. This happened on either March 15 or March 16, perhaps on both dates. The matter was raised again this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre, and I was amazed by the attitude of complacency shown by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) in answering the question. maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I, in common with the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) who has just taken his seat, had no idea that this motion would be made to-day. But representing as I do an agricultural constituency, it affords me an opportunity to place before the house some of my views in regard to the agricultural situation.
The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) saw fit during the course of the budget debate to deal with the question of the price ceiling in reference to agricultural products. He castigated the members of His Majesty's Loyal Opposition for indulging in sniping against the government's policy of fixation of prices. As I listened to his remarks in that connection I thought of a debate that was taking place in the legislature of Saskatchewan at about the same time. A motion was introduced there and voted upon on March 18 last. That motion was unanimously supported by every Liberal member in the Saskatchewan legislature. I read the pertinent portion of the motion having to do with the question of the ceiling on farm products:
That this assembly, recognizing the important place of the province of Saskatchewan in food production necessary to our war effort, strongly recommends to the federal government;
1. That further increases in prices paid to producers for essential food products be recognized as the most effective method of assuring production of necessary supplies.
Western Grain Crop

I pause to point out that that particular clause represents the idea which the Minister of Finance condemned in the most measured terms in this house the other day.
2. That appropriate action be taken to guarantee that the present general level of prices of meat animals, dairy and poultry products be maintained as minimum prices for the duration of the war and two years thereafter;
5. That, in view of the excellent prospects for sales of Canadian feed grain in the United States, we urge upon the federal government the desirability of removing existing maximum ceilings from these grains in order that prevailing prices in the United States may be fully reflected in prices paid to Canadian producers and that everything possible be done to facilitate the sale and transportation of Canadian feed grains to the United States.
It was a motion that directly attacked the price ceiling as far as farm products are concerned.
The names of those who voted for it, thereby calling upon the government to grant a higher level of agricultural prices, to grant parity prices for agricultural products, include every minister of the crown in the Saskatchewan legislature, many of them former colleagues of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in this government, a number of them members of the cabinet when he was premier of Saskatchewan. The Minister of Finance has condemned various members for asking that the farmer receive the same consideration as other industries, namely, a price that will pay his cost of production, give him a reasonable profit, and put him on a parity with the prices of the things he purchases. Most surprising of all, one of those who voted for the motion was Mr. Taggart, the former food administrator of Canada, who recently had control of food production in this country, and who more than anyone else should be in a position to speak with authority as to whether or not it is necessary in the interest of the prosperity and continuance of agriculture as a great influence in the war effort to have higher prices fixed for Canadian agricultural products.
To-day in Saskatchewan, with a provincial election in the offing, I presume the only discussion in connection with parity prices and the increase in agricultural prices above the present ceiling will be a reference, not to what was said recently by the Minister of Finance in this house, not to the attitude of the government of Canada, but to the attitude taken by the various ministers of the crown in the province of Saskatchewan on that motion.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not cost anything there.

Yes, it does not cost anything there. It represents to the 'people of

Saskatchewan that the Liberal party stands for one thing in the province although the federal party is diametrically opposed to it.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In other words, consistency demands that the Minister of Finance in this house shall uphold the orders made by the wartime prices and trade board, but in Saskatchewan expediency demands that the ministers of the crown there shall take a contrary attitude.
That motion was passed to emphasize that in order to ensure the necessary food production a course of increasing prices must be followed. The demand this year is for increased production in many lines. The Canadian farmer has made a tremendous contribution and is entitled to take pride in the contribution he has made. The fact that never has there been a suggestion by the Canadian farmer in the dark days of low prices which did not give him a fair and proper return that he would strike or do anything toward reducing production is something for which he is entitled to praise. It seems almost a truism to say that Canadian agricultural production must be increased and that the farmer is contributing much to the war effort of Canada and the united nations. If witness is needed to that fact, I refer to what the President of the United States said on January 12 last.
These were his words;
In spite of the handicaps under which American farmers worked last year, the production victory they won was among the major victories of the united nations in 1942. Food is a weapon in total war-fully as important in its way as guns or planes or tanks.
His words apply with equal force to the Canadian farmer.
At the same time the secretary of agriculture of the United States, Mr. Wickard, in speaking to the farmers of that country, is quoted as follows;
"You people are helping to bring victory sooner as you meet with your neighbours to-day." He added that farmers won the food production victory last year in spite of shortages of help and machinery and vexing but necessary government regulations.
"The devotion and determination and achievement of farmers was wonderful last year," he concluded. "This year the men on the battle lines are depending even more on American farmers. I know you will respond to that call."
The call that was made to United States farmers applies equally to Canadian farmers to-day. Increased production is necessary now in order to feed the nations. It will be needed

Western Grain Crop
in greater measure when the war is over, for then it will devolve upon Canada to assist in feeding a hungry world. Wheat will be in greater demand than ever before. Russia has had her granaries overrun. The Russian steppes must be rehabilitated before it will be possible for them to again produce wheat; and I believe that wheat properly stored to-day for the to-morrow that will come when this war is over, may very well be one of our greatest assets and one of the most important contributions Canada can make to the rehabilitation of the post-war world. To produce what is needed will require man-power, and I have no apology to offer for saying that at all times I have advocated a system of selective service that will ensure that every phase of the war effort receives its fair proportion of man-power. I repeat that food is important to-day. There is a terrible food shortage in Russia; according to a recent issue of the magazine Fortune, as long ago as last August and September there was no meat or butter in Moscow, and the average adult had lost fifteen pounds through inability to obtain nutritious food. Famine will soon appear unless food is sent to that country, and this condition prevails throughout Europe, where the nazis have adopted the policy of selective starvation of all the peoples who have come under their control. A revolutionary change is taking place in the economic set-up of Canada, particularly on the plains of the west, where coarse grains and pork products are being produced instead of wheat. After the war the changes which may take place in this economy must be carefully watched. Now is the time to plan to meet that changed economy.
In connection with the matter of price ceilings, the objection of the farmer is that agricultural prices were fixed at a time when these prices were below a parity level in regard to prices of other commodities. Prices of other commodities had advanced by the fall of 1941 to the point where there was a reasonable profit for those who produced them. I do not believe there is an individual who does not appreciate what has taken place under the system of price control in this dominion. Price control worked out in Australia, where it was adopted right at the beginning of the war. However, the farmer says that prices of his products are out of tune with prices received by other producers. The farmer cannot produce inferior farm products and get the same price he was paid for good products, whereas in many instances manufacturers are able to keep within the prices fixed during the basic period by turning out slightly different articles, of a lower or different grade
than produced in that period. That is the method by which, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) says, the prices of many products are kept within the ceiling. The farmer of western Canada believes that if there is to be a price ceiling at a time when he might expect to get much higher prices than he is now receiving, at least he has the right to demand the assurance that when the war is over, there will be a floor under the prices, in order to protect him against the lower prices which may follow as an aftermath of peace. Where is the policy of the government to-day in that respect? I have a great regard for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), but to-day he announced a policy of parts, of bits and pieces; some to-day, some to-morrow, and more is promised in forty-eight hours. That is the criticism one hears with regard to the agricultural policy of this government. It changes daily, weekly or monthly; and when an announcement is made by anyone in connection with agriculture, there is an immediate suspicion that some further change will be made which will be inconsistent with the announcement. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that fifteen days before butter rationing was brought into operation, the official in charge of the administration of the Department of Agriculture said there would be no butter rationing.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the dinner recess I was dealing with the necessity of planning in the Department of Agriculture. I come now to the next phase in connection with this matter, the production of flax. In the fall of 1942 the farmers were urged by the Department of Agriculture to aim at a higher flax production in 1943. As a matter of fact, at the dominion-provincial conference held in Ottawa in December it was recommended that there be a sixty-eight per cent increase in production. The farmers made plans to meet the demand, but in the month of January they were advised that that had been an error. The Minister of Agriculture then stated that the government would have to revise its plans and ideas in connection with the production of flax because there were not enough seed crushing plants in Canada and the United States to crush the surplus production over that of the previous year. It was only after a meeting with representatives of the United States that this fact was ascertained.
Western Grain Crop

This shows the lack, not only of long-time but of short-time planning in connection with agricultural production.
Last year the farmers were urged to sow coarse grains, particularly barley and oats. Naturally they believed that there would be a market available in Canada and the United States for that portion of their crop over and above that which might be fed in the production of hogs and live stock. As far as my own constituency is concerned, at the present time there are large quantities of these grains on hand. The farmers cannot dispose of them, and large quantities are still out in the field. Elevators are supposed to accept up to twenty bushels per acre, but they are refusing to make purchases because they have no space. In many instances no cars are available. There is a policy in effect to-day to provide for the shipment of a portion of this feed to eastern Canada, and I suggest that that policy should be extended. Something more should be done before it is too late, in order to assure these farmers, who relied on government promises that a market would be available and in consequence entered into greater production of oats and barley, shall not suffer. Those who relied on the government promises last year are now in a desperate position.
Most of the large farmers and many of the smaller ones cannot sow wheat in 1943 on account of the fourteen-bushel limit which has been imposed; they cannot do so because of the quantities of wheat they have on hand from the 1942 crop. They cannot sow coarse grains and the flax question is still in doubt. If there is any failure in production in the dominion as a whole, it is due to the fact that the farmers cannot place any reliance upon the announced plans of the government. When the Minister of Agriculture spoke in Saskatoon on January 15 he announced certain plans in connection with the production of wheat, oats, barley and rye. There was to be a decrease in the production of all these grains, but an increase in the production of mixed grains. There was to be no increase in the production of flax, but there was to be an increase in the production of hay and clover and a pronounced increase in the production of alfalfa. According to the news report of the British United Press, the minister went on to say:
Mr. Gardiner stated that the price inducement to meet these goals and acreage payments will be revealed to-day.
The Minister of Finance takes the stand that there shall be no increase in prices of agricultural products, and warns that if there is an increase or if more purchasing power is made available to the farmers, the price ceiling will be destroyed. On the other hand, as I

have pointed out, we have the legislature of Saskatchewan and the ministers of the crown of that province unanimously supporting a proposal and resolution to increase the prices for farm products. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that any lecture he has in mind to give with reference to those who support a policy of increased prices for agricultural products should be given to the Hon. Mr. Taggart and to the other ministers of the crown of Saskatchewan who support the party that he represents. Let me follow this a little further. These responsible men in the Liberal party in Saskatchewan voted in favour of the following resolution:
That in implementing the foregoing policies, we recommend to the federal government the payment of subsidies where, necessary to maintain price ceilings on consumer goods.
The payment of subsidies to the producer will increase the purchasing power in the hands of the farmer. If this policy has been found efficacious in so far as such goods as coffee, tea, oranges and the like are concerned, why should the subsidy system be restricted to industry or to the producers of these commodities and be denied to agriculture?

speechtext: The principle is the same.
