maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I appreciate that, but further subsidies are recommended by the legislature of Saskatchewan for the purpose of increasing prices paid to producers of essential food products. They suggest that such policy be recognized as the most effective method of assuring the production of necessary supplies. I would remind the Minister of Finance that the records show that agriculture progresses through a series of ups and downs; at one time prices are high and at another they are low. During the up periods the farmer has an opportunity of earning sufficient to tide him over the periods when his profits will be reduced to nil. If the government adheres to its policy that it will not increase farm prices to the level of the prices of other commodities as of the basic period, then I suggest that the farmers of Canada have a right to demand that when the war is over, the prices they will receive will be no lower than the present price level.
I mention in that connection that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, whose desire it is to serve the people of Canada and to improve and enlarge Canada's war effort, came to Ottawa during the month of February and

Western Grain Crop
made certain representations to the government. According to the press reports they were received by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other members of the cabinet and were assured that their representations would receive earnest consideration. The Prime Minister expressed the government's appreciation of the efforts of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to cooperate in the agricultural war effort, but as yet nothing has been done to carry the recommendations that were made into effect.
I submit that the time has come for the guaranteeing of live-stock prices for the duration of the war and two years thereafter in order to ensure continued expanding production, and that there should be a resumption of operations of the Wartime Food Corporation on the same lines as were followed during last July and August in order to- ensure that beef cattle in Canada shall bring prices reasonably related to prices in the United States. It is impossible to explain to the farmers of Canada, with a joint board on agriculture composed of representatives of Canada and the United States, why it is that there should be such different prices in Canada and the United States for farm commodities. Furthermore, I think the time has come for the inauguration of a comprehensive soil conservation survey as a national responsibility. The government should encourage cooperative enterprise in order that a larger portion of the consumer dollar shall be returned to the producer than would otherwise be the case. A time like this when the farmer is being asked to contribute to the war effort, and is doing it so willingly, is, in my opinion, not the time or occasion for the government to interfere with the growth of cooperative enterprise in Canada by the imposition of income taxation upon cooperative farm institutions.
The attitude of the Progressive Conservative party is set forth in its platform, and is that the farmer has a just cause for complaint in the prices that he is receiving. The Searle index shows, .starting with an index number of 100 for 1913-14, that 147 items representing commodities that the farmer buys are now 53-7 per cent higher than in that year, while the price of wheat is now only 5-5 per cent higher than it was in the same year. The purchasing power of a bushel of wheat is therefore only 68-6 per cent of what it was in 1913-14.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Searle Grain company's most- recent figure is 78 per cent.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What the hon.
gentleman says is perfectly correct. The figures I have here were those of some time ago.
I pass on to the question of man-power on the farms. Travel all over the prairie provinces to-day and you will find that most of the farms are almost depleted of man-power. The record of enlistments in the western provinces, as far as the farmer is concerned, compares with enlistments from any other class or group anywhere in this dominion. I know what numbers from my own constituency are listed from time to time in the casualty lists of the Royal Air Force and the Royal Canadian Air Force. I point this out, too, to those who say we need a united Canada in this war, that in these casualty lists of the air force will be seen many names of Ukrainians, Scandinavians and those of German origin who have enlisted from western Canada. These people have gone from our farms.
The objection which the farmer of western Canada has to the government's man-ipower policy is that it has no policy, that there has been no consistency, that the application of the National Resources Mobilization Act has been unfair in that it has in- many instances resulted in taking the last son from the farm from which the other sons have already gone overseas while in adjoining areas three and more brothers do not receive a call. To-day we are approaching a point where unless something is done agriculture cannot continue to measure up to its responsibility. What should be done?
In the United States Mrs. Roosevelt some time ago enunciated a policy which is now being applied, namely, the mobilization of a women's land army similar to that now working in Great Britain. Next, mobilization and training under government supervision of low-income farmers. They have mobilized in the United States an army of these men who have voluntarily assumed the responsibility of citizenship in assisting to keep u.p agricultural production. These men are given training and are moved back and forth during the seasons of maturing crops.
I do not think we have arrived at a point yet where it is necessary to follow the course that has been taken in the United States of bringing in labour from outside the nation. But I do believe that by now, in the month of March, 1943, sufficient time has elapsed since the beginning of this war for the government to be a-ble to announce to this house and the people of this country how many men there are available in Canada for agriculture. But a survey has not been made excepting on paper and in anticipation. I asked questions in the house on- March 1 in regard to the mobilization of our man-power and whether a survey had been made and
Western Grain Crop

have not yet received an answer. The reason must be that the government has no statistics on the subject to place before the house and the country. The first thing that must be done now, in my opinion, is to survey the situation. It is late, but let us do something now instead of postponing action until the day when we shall find ourselves in a dilemma of having no manpower on the farms. A step was made in the right direction early in February by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) when he sent out his letter of instructions respecting the call-up of farmers. But letters and instructions sent to boards and the like do not get results unless there is insistence on the part of the government that results be secured.
I hope that within the next week or so we can get a definite announcement of policy on this subject from the Minister of Labour. I know he is overworked, but I trust that an announcement will be made so that the farmer not only in western Canada but everywhere in the dominion will know what labour will be available to him during the coming summer. Furthermore I think, having regard to the fact that wheat and coarse grains farmers operate on a quota, something should be done to finance the farmers' crop while it remains on their farms. This was recommended by the Canadian Council of Agriculture. A system of this kind is being followed in the United States. To-day many farmers are unable to carry on because the quota which they have sold, perhaps no more than eight bushels to the acre, is insufficient to pay the cost of production, including labour, and to allow them anything over. In the United States, in order to encourage production, short-term loans have been established under the regional agricultural credit corporation, and $225 million has been made available at an interest rate of five per cent. I believe the same course will have to be followed in Canada if we are to secure the agricultural production which is necessary to ensure a continuing war effort on our part.
Furthermore, something should be done at this time in respect of the quantities of damp wheat which are to be found on farms all over western Canada. The wheat board should be urged to handle and dispose of this wheat in preference to wheat not in the same condition, so that spoilage and loss will be reduced to the minimum.
These are a few suggestions. I see that my time has almost elapsed. It is important to-day to realize that food is as necessary as other war materials are to the war effort; that without an adequate supply, the fight is hopeless.

The government has done much in connection with, and in the encouragement of munitions production. I ask that the same encouragement be given to agriculture as has been assured to industry producing other needed war requirements.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
During the dinner recess I was considering the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). The motion was that I leave the chair for the house to go into supply; and the hon. member for Melfort moved, seconded by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted:
"This house desires to record its opinion that before the marketing policy announced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on January 29 with respect to the 1943-44 crop is put into effect it be revised to bring it into conformity with the needs of agriculture so that the latter may be enabled to make its full contribution to the war effort."
The amendment refers to a statement which was made in the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) and which will be found on page 11 of Hansard of January 29 last. The minister stated:
In order to make provision for the required acreage we are asking farmers to reduce their wheat acreage by not less than 3,000,000 acres. To encourage this, the Minister of Agriculture will submit amendments to the Wheat Acreage Reduction Act, 1942, to provide payment of $2 an acre on each acre by which land seeded to wheat in 1943 is less than land seeded to wheat in 1940 based on the same acreage. If there is new breaking involved, 80 per cent of it will be counted as wheat and 20 per cent as coarse grains. No payment will be made in respect of abandoned land.
The amendment contemplates a revision of the government's agricultural policy, which is part of its financial policy. It can be assumed from the terms of the amendment that it means an addition to the expenditures proposed by the government as I have read them from Hansard and1 as stated in the house by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
There is another feature to which I must refer the house. As reported in Votes and Proceedings of February 23 last, page 93, there was an amendment moved to the address by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon):
And on the proposed motion of Mr. Graydon, seconded by Mr. Green, in amendment thereto: That the following words be added to the address:-
"We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that this house regrets that Your Excellency's advisers have failed (a) to provide an adequate plan for the effective use of Canada's man and woman power; (b) to adopt and carry through

Western Grain Crop
a national labour policy which will ensure maximum production and give to labour its rightful position as one of the major partners in our Canadian democracy; and-
This is the important part.
- (c) to provide adequate measures whereby Canadian agriculture can make its maximum war contribution and receive a fair share of the national income."
The amendment, as I pointed out, though in slightly altered form and with slightly different phraseology, contains the same conclusion as was contained in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition to the address in reply to the speech from the throne; and therefore citation 384 of Beauchesne will apply. The citation in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms provides as follows:
It is a rule in both houses, which is essential to the due performance of their duties that no question or bill shall be offered that is substantially the same as one on which their judgment has already been expressed in the current session.
The judgment of the house has already been expressed on the same question, as contained in the amendment of the leader of the opposition.
On the ground, therefore, that the proposed amendment involves an expenditure of money greater than that declared by the government for the purpose, and on the ground that the house has already expressed its opinion with regard to a similar proposal as contained in the amendment, I would have to rule it out of order.
I also refer the house to citation 559 of Beauchesne:
The constitutional principle which vests in the crown the sole responsibility of incurring national expenditure, forbids an increase by the commons of a sum demanded on behalf of the crown for the service of the state. This principle, however, is apparently disregarded when the recommendation of the crown is given to a resolution empowering the expenditure of public money which, framed in general terms, places no limitation on the amount of expenditure to be authorized by the resolution.
Here the amendment means an increase in the expenditure as stated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and therefore is contrary to that rule of the house.
I therefore rule the amendment out of order.
I may add that it seems to me that the amendment, while it is irregular, is also unnecessary, because the debate which is now taking place may continue on the motion to go into supply.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It does not stop the debate.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was a little disappointed with the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in that he did not give us something constructive by way of conclusion of his excellent remarks.
I believe it was Edward Blake who said that the duty of an opposition was to assist the government by constructive criticism. I take it for granted that constructive criticism would embody some help. The hon. member complained, as all of us who have our granaries full of grain, and some of it piled in the fields do, that we cannot get rid of it. He led us right up to the fourteen-bushel quota, and I thought he was about to tell us where we would go from there. At that point, however, he turned the whole matter back into the lap of the government, and said that the responsibility was theirs.
Then he dealt with the matter of damp grain. I agree that that is a real problem. But again he did not give us one word as to what he would do if he were dealing with damp grain. I am sure the wheat board is doing the best it can with the most difficult problem western Canada has ever known. When you find crops, such as we had in my district, ranging from 45 to 55 bushels of wheat per acre, barley running about 70 bushels, and oats at from 80 to 100 bushels, you have indeed an extraordinary situation, and a condition so different from any we have had in the past that naturally our problem is one with which no one can deal adequately.
In other respects I agreed largely with the hon. member's remarks. Something must be done to improve conditions in western Canada. I noted a few days ago in the press that the civil service is to be dealt with by way of bonus, and that incomes up to $3,000 are to be included. I have no particular criticism with regard to a decision of that kind, but I must say that a civil servant with an income of $3,000 is so much better off than the average farmer who has a lot of grain on his farm and does not know what he is to do with it, or whose grain may be out under the snow, unharvested, or who may have been subjected to the many other vicissitudes which beset the way of the western farmer, that I do feel if we can find money to pay bonuses to people with incomes of $3,000 we certainly should be able to find money with which to further subsidize the farmers. Long since have I argued, both in the house and out of it, that as long as we had a system of tariffs, and all those other systems which go with tariffs, and which taken together make
Western Grain Crop

up our present economy in which urban industries are supported by fiscal and many other arrangements not enjoyed by our farmers, we should subsidize agriculture up to the same level.
Where do we find all the good homes in Canada? Do we find them out on the farm where the people do most of the work? No, we do not. We find them in our cities, and very often they are lived in by parasites who make no particular contribution to the betterment of society. These are facts which cannot be refuted. Will anyone say for one moment that an accountant or a lawyer- and I am not pointing at the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier)-renders even twenty-five per cent of the service to the state rendered by the average good1 farmer? We have to revise our thinking in regard to agriculture or, before long, we shall not have any farmers.

It has grown up to a great extent on the backs of the western farmers, and the eastern farmer has made his contribution as well.

That means an over-all cost of $100 a month for each man. Two or three men on a farm at $100 a month means an expenditure of $200 or $300 for hired help. speechtext:

paid on fifty-cent oats.
I should like to make a few suggestions to the government. I do not know whether my suggestions will register, but I believe that with wage levels as they are to-day, circumscribed as we are by price ceilings-with the principle of which I agree fully-we should have a guaranteed price on flax of not less than $3 a bushel. Less than $3 will not take care of the risks involved in the growing of that crop. I have been growing flax for the last twenty years, and I have found that its yield varies from five to twenty-five bushels to the acre. We had a twenty-five bushel crop last year, and it would seem likely that we might have a six-bushel crop this year. A six-bushel crop at $2.25 gross means about $1.80. It cannot be grown for that. I say it cannot be grown for less than $3 a bushel, taking the average yield of about six bushels over a long-range period. I do not think it will be possible to grow wheat this year for ninety cents a bushel-although I am not much interested in wheat. It should be at least $1.35.
Comparing our live stock prices with those of the United States I was surprised to find that the basic price of bacon hogs in Canada is exactly the same, dressed, as it is in Chicago, live weight, namely sixteen cents a pound. In other words, the United States farmer gets about twenty cents for his hogs, dressed, while we get only sixteen cents for ours. The same is true of steers. They sell for sixteen cents in Chicago, and bring only twelve cents in Canada.
Something was said this afternoon with regard to wheat. There is about a 45-cent differential between the price of wheat in Chicago and1 the price in Canada. Of course in any calculation one makes of prices in Canada and in the United States he must remember the duty of forty-two cents a bushel on- all wheat going to United States.
While I do not wish to take up much time to-night, I should like now to draw a comparison between that portion of the national income going to agriculture, and that going to labour. We hear a good deal about labour of late. They have their problems, yes. The farmer, about thirty per cent of the population of Canada, with all his investment, running to I think about $2-5 billion in 1942 got 15-3 per cent of the national income while labour got 63-1 per cent, or four times as much, with less than half the population.
Speaking of farm debt. While debt adjustment is not so important in the district which I represent, because we have greater continuity in returns than some other sections of the

Western Grain Crop
west, I believe that in the light of conditions in Saskatchewan and Alberta there is some need of debt adjustment. In some instances it may mean complete wiping out of the debt.
I wish now to refer to the income tax on cooperatives. I cannot believe that the government is serious in the thought of imposing income tax on cooperatives. If that is done it will just drive the cooperatives back to a purely cooperative basis to where they belong. Some have departed slightly; as an example in the drought and depression years the Manitoba cooperative elevator association, out of concern for the elevators in the dried-out districts, decided for the time being to form their association into what we call line elevator companies in order to pool the resources of all the elevators to maintain elevators in operation in the drought areas. It will just drive the cooperatives back to where they ought to be, and then there will be no profits to tax. I hope the government will think twice before attempting to impose income tax on something that is not there, because in a cooperaive there is really no residue on which to impose taxation.
Something has been said in regard to the need for fuller cooperation in respect of agriculture. It has been said that what we need in this country is political cooperatives. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have frequently urged that if the cooperatives would associate themselves with the socialist party of Canada, it would be to their advantage. A few years ago I had- the privilege of having lunch- with the minister of agriculture for Norway. I made good use of the two hours we were lunching by asking questions. I inquired how they had succeeded so well with their cooperatives in Norway. "I suppose you are pretty m-uch socialist?" I said. "Oh, no, no," he said; "we a-re the very opposite. Socialism would kill cooperation." I hope my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation get that. He said, " We are all for private enterprise in Norway."

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? Did he not belong to this crowd once himself?

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not as far as I know. There was an organization known as the Progressive movement, of which my hon. friend and his friends have stolen the name-time is a great wonder worker, and it may be that my hon. friend and his friends will yet be in the C.C.F. movement down at the other end. The Progressive movement was very successful- in its day, ddd a great deal of good and justified its existence in this house. The minister of agriculture for Norway, a man
who should know, was most emphatic in his belief that the cooperatives could live and prosper only under a system of private enterprise.
I wish the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) were in his seat at the moment. I believe in his price ceiling; I am all for it. Probably no group of men could have done a better job than he and the prices board have done. But I do not think we should maintain stability and prevent inflation at the expense of one class only. The farmer to-day is paying the long price for his country's financial stability. That is not fair. We should lift the lid on some agricultural products. We should put the farmer at least on a par with others in the community, particularly organized labour.

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Has the hon. member the idea that the farmer is not getting a fair deal as far as the price ceiling is concerned?

maintopic: MARKETING OF WESTERN GRAIN CROP-AMENDMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have just said so. I believe that flax should be not less than $3 a bushel, I do not believe it can be grown successfully for less. There should also be a higher price for wheat. I suggest $1.35.
If we are to maintain agriculture and keep the young people on our farms we must give greater attention to our farm economy. An hon. member in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group this afternoon, I think it was the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castleden), referred to the coming home of the soldiers after the war. That is something to which we must give some thought. The hon. member quoted a figure of eighty or ninety cents an hour for labour in the factories and the farmer getting twenty cents. Surely we should- do something about that.
